item.text: {"text":"Published evidence supports separating recency dependence from sensitivity to earlier sequence order. “Robust Training of Sequential Recommender Systems with Missing Input Data” explains why removing the final observation changes the prediction context and can make the original target poorly aligned with next-item training; degradation alone therefore does not establish useful longer-range temporal reasoning ([paper](https://assets.amazon.science/ea/6b/d2f305e64d1394abe7839be6e976/robust-training-of-sequential-recommender-systems-with-missing-input-data.pdf)). “An Analysis of Sequential Recommendation Datasets” compares shuffled and chronological training histories while retaining validation/test targets, but this differs from fixing a trained GRU4Rec and preserving its final observed input during inference perturbations ([paper](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-2955/paper8.pdf)). Neither directly establishes the proposed diagnostic’s result for this benchmark.\n\nRecommended diagnostic, inferred from these findings: freeze each category’s trained GRU4Rec; shuffle only preceding nonpadding items while preserving the final observed item, history length, item multiset, target and candidate set. Separately delete equal numbers of recent versus older interactions while retaining the final observation; preserve surviving order, compact and left-pad identically. Include unchanged-input controls, repeated seeded shuffles, and final-item deletion as a separate recency stress test. Measure paired changes in target rank, reciprocal rank and HR@10 on identical validation users and candidates; report uncertainty and category-level results before macro averaging. Read from the final nonpadding position. Ranking changes establish sensitivity; consistent deterioration establishes predictive usefulness under that perturbation. Strong final-item deletion effects with weak final-preserving shuffle effects suggest recency dependence, while stronger recent-than-older deletion effects suggest useful recent context without proving order dependence."}
